lede: Burning pain or the feeling of a pebble under the ball of your foot, often between the third and fourth toes, can point to Morton's neuroma.
what_it_is: Morton's neuroma is a thickening of the tissue around one of the small nerves that run between the long bones of the forefoot out to the toes. According to the American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons, it most often develops between the third and fourth toes. The nerve passes under a ligament that links the metatarsal bones, and when it is squeezed there over and over, the surrounding tissue swells and thickens.

The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons reports that Morton's neuroma is around 8 times more common in women than men and typically affects people between the ages of 30 and 60. Running, tennis and other court sports, and long days in narrow or high-heeled shoes all put repeated pressure on the ball of the foot. If you are active around Jupiter, Juno Beach or Abacoa, those are the habits worth mentioning to your podiatrist.
symptoms: Burning, sharp or stabbing pain in the ball of the foot
A feeling like walking on a pebble or marble
Tingling, pins and needles or numbness in two neighboring toes
A sense that your sock is bunched up under the foot
Pain that builds with activity or in tight, high-heeled shoes
Relief when you stop, take off your shoe and rest the foot
A clicking feeling in the forefoot
causes: Narrow, tapered or high-heeled shoes that compress the forefoot
Running, court sports and other high-impact activities
Flat feet, high arches or very flexible feet

how_therapy_helps.intro: Most treatment for Morton's neuroma aims to take pressure off the irritated nerve. The American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons lists padding, icing, orthotics, activity changes and wider shoes as first steps, with injections when symptoms persist. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons reports that conservative care, such as footwear changes, activity changes and orthotics, may provide some degree of relief in up to about 50% of patients, so some people go on to injections, nerve-targeted procedures or surgery. ACFAS reserves surgery for patients who have not responded adequately to nonsurgical treatment.
methods: Pads placed in the shoe support the metatarsal arch, which ACFAS says lessens the pressure on the nerve with each step.
A wide toe box and a lower heel give the forefoot room. ACFAS and Mayo Clinic both point to narrow and high-heeled shoes as a key source of pressure.
ACFAS notes that custom orthotic devices provide the support needed to reduce pressure and compression on the nerve.
Icing helps reduce swelling, and cutting back on activities that pound the forefoot gives the nerve a chance to settle, per ACFAS.
ACFAS lists injections of cortisone, local anesthetic or other agents for persistent symptoms. AAOS also describes chemical and radiofrequency ablation that target the nerve.
When conservative care fails, AAOS describes removing the thickened nerve (neurectomy) or releasing the ligament that presses on it (decompression).

first_visit: At your first visit, the podiatrist asks where the pain sits, what it feels like and which shoes or activities set it off. The doctor presses and squeezes across the forefoot to try to reproduce your symptoms, a check AAOS calls the web-space compression test, and may feel a click between the metatarsal bones. The exam also looks for bunions, hammertoes or an arch shape that adds pressure, and the doctor may order imaging to rule out other causes.
recovery: Recovery time depends on how long symptoms have been present and which treatment works for you. Some people improve with shoe changes and padding, while others need injections or a procedure. After surgery, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says patients wear a stiff-soled shoe at first and typically return to normal shoes by 4 weeks. AAOS also notes that symptoms may return in around 5 to 20% of patients and need additional treatment, which is why follow-up visits and good footwear habits matter after treatment.
self_care: Wear shoes with a wide toe box and a low heel, and set aside narrow or pointed styles for now.
Ice the ball of the foot to help calm swelling, with a cloth between the ice pack and your skin.
Cut back on running, jumping and court sports that pound the forefoot until you are seen.
Take off your shoes and rest the foot when the burning starts.
An over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medicine may help if it is safe for you.
see_a_doctor: Foot pain that lasts longer than a few days
Burning in the ball of the foot that does not improve after changing shoes or activities
Pain that continues after two weeks of home care, or keeps getting worse

faqs.q: Can Morton's neuroma go away on its own?
faqs.a: Symptoms can ease when pressure on the nerve is reduced, which is why wider shoes, padding and rest come first. Cleveland Clinic states that the neuroma itself does not simply go away, so ongoing pain is a reason to be examined. ACFAS says the best time to see a foot and ankle surgeon is early in the development of symptoms, and Mayo Clinic advises against ignoring foot pain that lasts longer than a few days.

faqs.q: Can I keep running with Morton's neuroma?
faqs.a: The American College of Foot and Ankle Surgeons recommends avoiding activities that put repetitive pressure on the neuroma until the condition improves, and running is one of the most common culprits. Cleveland Clinic suggests lower-impact exercise as a way to reduce stress on the forefoot. Your podiatrist can help you plan a gradual return once the nerve has calmed down.

faqs.q: Do cortisone shots work for Morton's neuroma?
faqs.a: They can help for a while. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons reports that corticosteroid injections provide short-term relief in about 50 to 70% of patients with Morton's neuroma, though long-term relief is less common. Injections are usually tried after shoe changes, padding and orthotics. Results vary from person to person, and a podiatrist will discuss how many injections are reasonable and what comes next if relief does not last.

faqs.q: What shoes are best for Morton's neuroma?
faqs.a: Look for shoes with a wide, roomy toe box and a low heel. ACFAS advises avoiding narrow-toed shoes, and Mayo Clinic notes that high heels and tight shoes place extra pressure on the toes and ball of the foot. A shoe with enough room in the forefoot also leaves space for a metatarsal pad or custom orthotic if your podiatrist recommends one.

faqs.q: When is surgery needed for Morton's neuroma?
faqs.a: Surgery is considered when nonsurgical treatment has not given adequate relief, according to ACFAS. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes two main approaches: removing the affected section of nerve (neurectomy) or releasing the ligament that compresses it (decompression), with most studies reporting success rates of 80 to 95%. After surgery, AAOS says most people return to normal shoes by about 4 weeks.

notes_for_reviewer: This page quotes AAOS outcome figures (conservative care up to about 50%, steroid injections about 50 to 70%, surgery 80 to 95%, recurrence 5 to 20%). They are national figures attributed to AAOS, not practice outcomes. Remove them if you prefer no percentages on the page.
Please confirm the practice offers metatarsal padding, custom orthotics and cortisone or local anesthetic injections for neuroma. They are described as common podiatric options attributed to ACFAS.
Please confirm whether the surgeons perform neurectomy, decompression, or chemical or radiofrequency ablation. The page describes these generically per AAOS.
AAOS calls ultrasound the preferred imaging method. The page only says the doctor 'may order imaging' and makes no in-office ultrasound or X-ray claim.

MLS laser is omitted because no fetched source supports it for Morton's neuroma. Fact-check correction: AAOS OrthoInfo does mention extracorporeal shockwave therapy and platelet-rich plasma as second-line add-ons to other treatments, with limited research showing possible benefit.
